transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-15
Start: 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Arjun Patel (Redwood SE), Lucas Rivera (Redwood Infra), Priya Sundar (Blue River Labs, ML Platform), Tom Nguyen (BRL SRE), Dana Morales (BRL Head of ML)
Shared artifacts: short deck (link: https://redwood.app/decks/cuda-graph-profiling), bench csv placeholder (s3://brl-benchmarks/cuda-graph/), kernel flamegraphs (to be attached)

Summary:
Redwood SE walked through kernel selection and CUDA-graph capture tradeoffs for high-throughput LLM inference. Primary focus: TensorRT-LLM (TRT-LLM) kernels vs vLLM optimized kernels, effects of CUDA graphs on latency tail, and KV cache behavior under prefix-heavy workloads. Customer asked about on-prem/VPC constraints (no internet egress for some clusters) and quantization regressions. Outcome: Redwood to run targeted A100/H100 runs with customer's sample traffic and deliver p50/p95/p99 numbers plus kernel-level traces.

Topics covered:
- Kernel selection heuristics (cutlass vs cuBLAS vs TensorRT fused kernels)
- CUDA graph capture overhead and warmup vs per-request dynamic capture
- vLLM batching primitives and its memory/latency tradeoffs
- KV cache sharding & prefix caching implications for latency and memory
- Quantization (FP16 / INT8 / 4-bit) accuracy vs perf
- On-prem / VPC constraints: NVLink, multi-gpu, KMS for keys

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro then Arjun will jump to the kernel-level stuff. Priya, do you want to say 30 seconds on the workload?
[00:14] Priya Sundar: Sure, thanks Maya. We're evaluating inference for a chat assistant internal to BRL — about 60% short queries (<=64 tokens), 30% mid (128-512), and 10% long (>1024). Peak qps around 280, sustained 120. Our infra is mostly on-prem A100 fleet with some H100 in the cloud. We also have strict no-egress constraints for PHI workloads.
[00:42] Arjun Patel: Great — that mix matters a lot for batching and KV cache hit rates. We'll explain tradeoffs with CUDA graphs and kernel selection. Quick note: I'll sometimes say 'KV cash' — ignore transcription quirk.
[01:05] Arjun Patel: Starting at a high level — TRT-LLM gives highly fused attention+ffn kernels and uses TensorRT's kernel selection. For short sequences and small batch sizes, those fused kernels reduce kernel launch overhead and can hit better p50 latency. vLLM, by contrast, optimizes scheduling and batching strategy and has extremely low-overhead attention loops in some configurations. It tends to be better if you want dynamic batch packing at higher throughput.
[01:47] Tom Nguyen: For us the p99 tail matters more than avg. Curious how CUDA graphs change the tail?
[01:58] Arjun Patel: Good question. CUDA graphs reduce per-step launch overhead — you capture a static graph of ops and then replay. That helps a lot when the computational graph is stable: same sequence length and batch shape. But if you have variable seq lengths or dynamic prompts, capture overhead or need for multi-graph variants becomes a management headache. With TRT-LLM + CUDA graphs on A100 we saw p99 drop by ~20-30% in some synthetic runs for seq=128, batch=8. However, when you add KV cache warmups for long contexts, the first few steps may still spike because of memory allocation patterns and cache fills.
[02:47] Priya Sundar: So is the capture done per request shape? That sounds like explosion of graphs if we have many seq lengths.
[02:57] Arjun Patel: Yes — naive capture is per (batch_size, seq_len). Redwood's serving runtime will try to canonicalize shapes: pad/pack to a small set of shapes and use dynamic batching to reduce the combinatorial explosion. We typically keep a small shape set (e.g., 32/128/512) and route requests accordingly. That keeps CUDA graphs manageable. But there's a tradeoff: padding increases compute, affecting throughput.
[03:30] Dana Morales: What about kernel selection? I keep hearing 'cutlass' and 'cublas' and 'TensorRT fused'. How do you pick?
[03:40] Arjun Patel: Kernel selection is heuristics + microbenchmarks. Cutlass-based kernels (fused GEMMs) are great for certain matrix sizes — they let us tune tile sizes and exploit tensor cores. cuBLAS is reliable for large GEMMs. TensorRT fused kernels often do attention + ffn fusion which reduces memory movement. Our runtime collects a small profile (matrix dims, seq length distribution) and picks the kernel that historically wins for those dims on the given GPU. The heuristic also considers memory bandwidth and expected KV cache behavior.
[04:21] Lucas Rivera: To add — we also factor in occupancy and SM sched. On H100 the larger tensor cores shift the sweet spot; a kernel that was best on A100 might not be best on H100. So we have a GPU-specific profile.
[04:44] Tom Nguyen: And multi-gpu? We plan to shard KV cache across two A100s with NVLink. Any gotchas?
[04:55] Arjun Patel: Sharding KV across GPUs can reduce per-GPU memory and enable longer contexts. But it introduces cross-gpu comms at each decode step unless you pipeline the kv retrieval. NVLink helps but still adds latency. For latency-sensitive single-request scenarios, single-GPU with quantization is usually simpler. For throughput and very long contexts, sharding is worth it if you can hide the communication via async memcpy and overlap compute.
[05:30] Priya Sundar: You mentioned quantization regressions. What have you observed?
[05:36] Arjun Patel: In our internal tests, 8-bit linear quantization with per-channel scales for weights (INT8) often holds up for generation quality on CODE- and chat-type tasks, but some models show hallucination increases at 4-bit schemes unless you do careful outlier handling or use mixed precision (e.g., FP16 for certain layers). We recommend running evals on a representative prompt set. Redwood Optimize can suggest quant profiles based on the eval delta.
[06:10] Dana Morales: Can you run quantized TRT-LLM with CUDA graphs safely?
[06:16] Arjun Patel: Yes — TRT-LLM supports mixed precision kernels and can be captured with CUDA graphs. The main caution is ensuring numeric determinism if you rely on bit-exact logs; truncation can shift timings slightly due to different kernel shapes and instruction mixes. Also INT8 kernels may trigger different kernel selection paths, so you'll want to re-profile after quantization.
[06:44] [08:00] Speaker 1 (Maya or generic): quick interjection — how do you handle KV cache eviction for multi-tenant hosts?
[08:09] Lucas Rivera: We use per-tenant memory quotas and an LRU-like prefix cache. For BRL with PHI workloads, we can pin certain tenants to dedicated pools (Redwood Dedicated model) so eviction isn't noisy.
[08:30] Priya Sundar: About VPC/on-prem — we can't send model artifacts outside. Can Redwood run an on-prem private control plane?
[08:41] Maya Chen: Yes — Redwood Private supports a VPC-only control plane and on-prem packages. For the benchmarks we'll provide a dockerized runner that you can execute in your air-gapped cluster — we'll only need the CSV and logs you permit to share.
[09:02] Arjun Patel: Back to micro-profiling — we recommend three traces: a) kernel-level timeline (ns resolution), b) CUDA graph capture trace showing memcpy/capture overhead, c) flamegraph of GEMM/attention ops. The flamegraph helps spot if time is dominated by GEMM compute vs memory copies. In some runs we saw dashtype memory copies (kv compaction) eating 15-20% of time at decode step 1.
[09:38] Tom Nguyen: Can you give an example numberset you expect to share?
[09:43] Arjun Patel: Example: seq=128, batch=8, model=7B fp16 on A100: p50 ~ 35ms, p95 ~ 120ms, p99 ~ 220ms, tokens/sec ~ 9k (these are synthetic). With CUDA-graph + TRT fused kernels, p95/p99 improved ~20-30%. For seq=1024, the numbers shift: throughput drops but batching helps; KV cache warmup causes first-step spikes. We'll produce real numbers from your workload.
[10:20] Priya Sundar: How do you handle variable-length requests in CUDA graphs without over-padding?
[10:28] Arjun Patel: Two strategies: 1) shape canonicalization (pack to small set of shapes, route), 2) dynamic capture that uses some small set plus fallbacks. Redwood's runtime prefers canonicalization with a fallback to non-capture execution for rare shapes. This minimizes graph count.
[11:05] Dana Morales: Are there open-source tooling tradeoffs? vLLM is OSS and has great packing. TRT-LLM is tied to NVIDIA stack. Does Redwood support both?
[11:16] Maya Chen: We support both in our catalog — the runtime can route to an internal TRT-LLM optimized variant or a vLLM optimized path depending on policy: cost-first vs latency-first. Customers like BRL often want a hybrid — TRT-LLM for stable low-latency paths and vLLM for bursty throughput.
[11:45] Arjun Patel: Also worth noting: vLLM's scheduler is excellent for dynamic packing, which reduces compute overhead when you have many small requests. But vLLM's attention implementation sometimes uses more CPU orchestration which can increase infra complexity for on-prem deployments.
[12:12] Tom Nguyen: About CUDA graph capture — is the capture time a measurable overhead in our env?
[12:18] Arjun Patel: Capture is typically a one-time cost per graph (microseconds to milliseconds depending on graph size). But if you capture on-demand at runtime for rare shapes, the capture latency can be visible to users. There is also memory usage for the captured graph kernel descriptors. We usually warm-up graphs during startup or during a warm traffic period.
[13:00] [18:30] Arjun Patel: We also ran experiments with CUDA Graphs + dynamic parallelism for attention where we pre-allocate KV buffers and avoid repeated small allocations. That improved p95 by about 10% in our bench for long contexts.
[14:05] Priya Sundar: Any specific recommendations for runtime config? We use batch-size soft limits and have a max latency SLO of 400ms p95.
[14:14] Arjun Patel: For your traffic I'd start with: canonical shapes [32, 128, 512], batch soft limit 16, max batching latency 60ms. Enable CUDA graphs for the canonical shapes. Use fp16 by default; run INT8 for candidate models and evaluate quality. For long-context heavy users, consider single-GPU with 4-bit quant+KV compaction or sharded KV if you need >64k tokens.
[15:02] Dana Morales: How about tooling to detect regressions after quantization?
[15:08] Arjun Patel: Redwood Optimize will run eval suites and surface a quality delta per prompt set. We also push diffed model outputs to a retention bucket for manual review. For critical prompts we can pin a canary traffic stream.
[15:35] Tom Nguyen: Any pitfalls with TensorRT's kernel selection when we update CUDA/drivers?
[15:40] Lucas Rivera: Yes — driver and CUDA versions can change kernel selection and perf. We recommend freezing a supported stack for production or running a short re-profile job in canary after driver updates. Our CI runs a lightweight microbench after driver updates to catch regressions.
[16:05] [25:00] Arjun Patel: Quick demo notes — I'll capture a small run now (not live) and then share artifacts: kernel timeline, captured cudaGraph sizes, and cutlass vs trt kernel choices.
[16:30] Priya Sundar: When you share the artifacts, can you include aflame graphs and a readme with lines that point to suspect kernels? That helps our SREs.
[16:40] Arjun Patel: Absolutely. We'll annotate the flamegraphs with kernel names and recommended mitigations (e.g., increase workspace size, change tile sizes, adjust batch packing).
[17:10] Maya Chen: Quick commercial note — if BRL wants dedicated pools for PHI workloads we can scope a Dedicated deployment; that avoids noisy multi-tenant eviction. We'll include cost-ballpark in the follow-up.
[18:00] Priya Sundar: For the on-prem runner, any special privileges required? We have strict security posture.
[18:06] Lucas Rivera: The runner needs access to GPUs and local KMS for models if you choose to keep keys on-prem. No external egress is required. We'll provide an air-gapped installer and logs can be written to a local S3-compatible endpoint.
[18:40] Dana Morales: Anything about fallback behavior if TRT-LLM kernels fail or OOM?
[18:45] Arjun Patel: The runtime has automatic fallbacks: if a CUDA graph run OOMs we fallback to non-captured execution or to a smaller shape. We also maintain model variants (quantized or smaller-context) for graceful degradation.
[19:12] [35:00] Priya Sundar: Curious about instrumentation overhead. If we enable kernel-level tracing in production what's the overhead?
[35:08] Arjun Patel: Fine-grained kernel tracing is expensive; we usually do it in short windows. Low-overhead metrics (per-route latency, token counts, batch sizes) are always on. Kernel-level traces are pulled during benchmarks or incident debugging.
[36:00] Tom Nguyen: Does Redwood provide NVLink-aware scheduling?
[36:06] Lucas Rivera: Yes, the runtime's placement logic is NVLink-aware. If GPUs on a host have NVLink we prefer local sharding to avoid PCIe cross-host costs. We'll expose placement hints in the config.
[37:00] Dana Morales: Any gotchas when moving from A100 to H100?
[37:06] Arjun Patel: On H100, some kernels that relied on smaller tile sizes become suboptimal. H100's Tensor Cores better use certain shape sizes; so re-profiling is essential. Also check cuBLASLt variations — some choice combos shift. We'll include both A100 and H100 runs.
[38:10] Priya Sundar: For our p95 400ms SLO, do you think canonicalization + CUDA graphs is the right default?
[38:18] Arjun Patel: Yes, provided you accept a small compute overhead from padding. The gain in reducing p99 spikes typically outweighs the padding cost for chat-like traffic. But we'll validate with your sample workload.
[39:00] Maya Chen: Let's recap immediate next steps.
[39:05] Maya Chen: Action 1 — Arjun runs TRT-LLM and vLLM end-to-end on A100/H100 using BRL sample traffic and shares CSV + flamegraphs.
[39:14] Maya Chen: Action 2 — Priya uploads sample traffic and grants S3 access.
[39:19] Maya Chen: Action 3 — Lucas confirms VPC/no-egress and NVLink settings and available nodes.
[39:26] Maya Chen: We'll tentatively meet on 2025-04-24 to review results.
[39:34] Tom Nguyen: Sounds good. Appreciate the concrete next steps.
[39:40] Dana Morales: Quick question — can we get a short writeup on recommended batch settings for each canonical shape?
[39:46] Arjun Patel: Yes we'll include a per-shape suggestions table and the reasons (tile sizes, expected p50/p95).
[40:00] [End notes]
Meeting ended ~15:32 UTC. Artifacts promised: bench csv, kernel flamegraphs, annotated trace, short config playbook for canonical shapes.
